ui.title: Customize
ui.subtitle: Change how documents look with a theme, or add new syntax and behavior with a plugin. Both are single files you drop into a folder; no build step and no restart. Every example on this page was loaded into the app to draw the screenshot next to it.

blocks.text: There are two kinds of extension, and each has its own folder:

items: **Theme**: a `.css` file in the themes folder. It styles the preview, HTML export and PDF.
**Plugin**: a `.js` file in the plugins folder. It adds syntax, rewrites the rendered page, or draws things into it.

blocks.text: The quickest way there is **Settings → Appearance → Open themes folder** (or **Settings → Plugins → Open plugins folder**). After you add or change a file, press **Reload** in the same tab. The app does not need to restart.
A theme is one CSS file. Its name, without `.css`, is what you pick in Settings → Appearance. Everything is scoped to `.markdown-body`, the element that holds the rendered page.
Start from a complete file

A custom theme replaces the built-in look rather than sitting on top of Default, so a file that only styles headings leaves everything else unstyled. The structural rules (spacing, list markers, full-width tables, page breaks) always apply. Colors, fonts, borders and backgrounds come from your theme. The simplest start is to copy the example below and change what you like.

blocks.alt: A document drawn with the rose theme: a dark red heading, pink table borders, and a chart and diagram in the same colors

blocks.text: What you can style

head: Selector
What it is
rows: The page itself: text color, background, font, and the custom properties below
Inline code, as opposed to code blocks
Code blocks. Token colors are covered below
Tables. Use `tbody tr:nth-child(even)` for zebra stripes
`:::note` and `:::warning` blocks. The heading text is in the `data-title` attribute, drawn by `::before`
Images that have a caption. `figcaption { display: none }` turns captions off
To-do checkboxes in lists, and the standalone ones
Containers for diagrams and charts. Use them for spacing, not colors (see the next two sections)

blocks.text: A rule works the same in the preview, in HTML export and in PDF. Put print-only changes in `@media print { … }`.
Code block colors

Code blocks are highlighted with Shiki, which writes two sets of colors onto every token as CSS variables, `--shiki-light` and `--shiki-dark`, plus `--shiki-light-bg` and `--shiki-dark-bg` for the block. The light set is used unless you say otherwise. A theme with a dark page can switch to the dark set:

blocks.label: CSS

blocks.text: Fonts

Noto Sans and Noto Serif, with their Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese, Japanese and Korean variants, ship with the app. `font-family: 'Noto Serif', 'Noto Serif TC', Georgia, serif` therefore looks the same on every computer. Any other font has to be installed on the computer that reads the document and is not embedded in an export.
Chinese, Japanese and Korean share many characters, and the first font in the list that has a character draws it. List the language you write in first (`TC`, then `SC`, then `JP`, then `KR`).
Charts are drawn into images while the document renders, so CSS rules cannot reach inside them. Instead a theme sets custom properties on `.markdown-body`, and the chart reads them when it is drawn.

head: Property
Meaning
rows: Colors of the series (or slices), in order. Defaults: `#4e79a7`, `#f28e2b`, `#59a14f`, `#e15759`, `#b07aa1`, `#9c755f`, `#76b7b2`, `#bab0ac`. With more series than colors they repeat
Titles, axis labels and legend. Defaults to the page's text color
Font family of the chart text. Defaults to the page's font

blocks.text: Overriding one chart

Form B (a `chart` code block) takes a full Chart.js configuration, so anything Chart.js supports is available for a single chart. A dataset that sets its own `backgroundColor` or `borderColor` keeps it; the theme only colors datasets that have none.
The configuration is YAML or JSON, so it cannot contain functions.

Diagrams use the same idea: `--mermaid-*` custom properties are passed to Mermaid as its theme variables. Setting any one of them switches Mermaid to its customizable `base` theme, and every variable you leave out is worked out from the ones you set. Set none and diagrams keep Mermaid's stock look.

head: Property
Meaning
rows: Fill, text and border of the main nodes. Start here
Second and third color families (each with `-text` and `-border`), used by other diagram types and by nested parts
Background behind the labels on arrows
Write `true` for a diagram palette meant for a dark page

blocks.text: Write colors as hex codes such as `#ffe4e6`, because Mermaid computes the shades it needs from them.

A plugin is one `.js` file in the plugins folder. It is an ES module whose **default export** is an object. Settings → Plugins lists every file with a switch (a switched-off plugin is never loaded) and shows the error if one fails to load.
What goes in the object

head: Field
What it does
rows: The name shown in the list. Defaults to the file name

Gives `:::name{attr=value}` and `::name` syntax an HTML element. Each entry is a function that receives `{ name, kind, attributes }` (`kind` is `text`, `leaf` or `container`) and returns `{ tagName, properties }`. What is written inside the block renders inside that element
Plugins for the Markdown syntax tree, in unified's format: a function, or `[function, options]`
Plugins for the HTML tree that run before code is highlighted. Use this to take over code blocks of your own language, as the built-in Mermaid and chart plugins do
Plugins for the HTML tree that run after highlighting
A string, or a function of the rendered HTML that returns one, so the styles can be left out when unused. It comes before the theme's CSS, so a theme can override it
`(root, { themeCss }) => void | Promise` runs on the rendered page in the preview, in HTML export and in PDF. Use it to draw things into placeholders or adjust the DOM
Markdown that explains your syntax. It is added to the syntax guide an AI assistant receives over MCP, so the assistant knows how to write it

blocks.text: Example 1: new syntax
This plugin adds `:::tip{title="…"}`. In `properties`, use HTML property names: `className`, and `dataTitle`, which becomes the attribute `data-title`.
Example 2: rewrite the HTML

A rehype plugin is a function that returns a function, which receives the tree and changes it. Plugins are loaded as stand-alone modules, so `import` of package names or other files does not work, and the tree is walked by hand. That takes about ten lines.
Example 3: after the page is drawn
`postRender` gets the rendered element and can do anything DOM code can. This one adds a reading time at the top, in the preview and in exports.

blocks.alt: A document with three plugins at work: a reading time at the top, an arrow after the external link, and a green tip box

blocks.text: Installing and removing

items: Put the file in the plugins folder and press **Reload** in Settings → Plugins.
If it fails to load, the reason appears under its name. Common causes are a syntax error or a missing `export default`.
To stop using one, switch it off in the list or delete the file.

blocks.text: **Only install plugins you trust.** A plugin runs with the same abilities as the editor's own page, including reading and saving files through the app.
